clue.text: Soften everything one included in paste

indicators.note: something included in a thing sits inside it, so the first words go within the spread named last

parts.note: pâté is a savoury paste spread on toast
everything is all of it
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A recipe tip: mix every ingredient into the paste to make it softer.
explanation.definitionFit: To palliate is to ease or mitigate pain or harshness, a close synonym of soften in that sense.

clue.text: Be rich enough to commission computer equipment?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for being comfortably wealthy and successful
second, playful meaning: to commission is to get something made, and IT is information technology kit

explanation.surface: Only someone wealthy can afford to have bespoke computers built for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: HAVE IT MADE, that is, get the IT built to order.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning one is wealthy and set for life, so it matches being rich enough.

clue.text: Place for tobogganing — that is sport involving cold, note

indicators.note: a thing involving another takes it in, so the Latin abbreviation wraps around the temperature letter

parts.note: i.e., the abbreviation of id est, that is
C for cold, as on a tap
Rugby Union
N as an abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: Describes a frosty winter-sports spot, with a stray musical note thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice run is a frozen track down which toboggans and sleds slide, so it is a venue for that sport.

clue.text: US chap — he will appear in unsatisfactory opera

indicators.note: the man and the pronoun turn up inside the word for poor quality, which encloses them

parts.note: a lame excuse is an unsatisfactory one
bo is American slang for a pal or fellow
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American man shows up in a weak operatic production.
explanation.definitionFit: La Bohème is Puccini's famous opera about bohemian artists in Paris, so it is an example of an opera.

clue.text: French are supporting one date, a significant date

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part supporting another sits underneath it, so the French verb comes last

parts.note: Roman numeral for one
D as an abbreviation for date
es is the French for are, as in tu es

explanation.surface: Reads like French speakers propping up someone's diary entry.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March (the 15th) is the date Julius Caesar was assassinated, hence significant.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the ides fell mid-month, and the Ides of March is a famously momentous day in history.

clue.text: Tumours in significant ratio linked to college

indicators.note: items linked together are joined end to end, so the college goes beside the constant

parts.note: short for polytechnic, a former type of British college
pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter

explanation.surface: Sounds like a medical statistic about growths at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: A poly was a British polytechnic college, many of which became universities in 1992.
explanation.definitionFit: Polypi is a plural of polyp, a small growth on a mucous membrane, so it names tumours.

clue.text: Du Maurier novel not popular around Caribbean nation

definitions.note: adjective: relating to or about that nation

indicators.note: not popular says drop the word meaning in fashion from the title

parts.note: Jamaica Inn, Daphne du Maurier's 1936 novel set in Cornwall
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: A literary note: a du Maurier book that failed to sell in the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caribbean nation' looks like the definition, but it would give the noun; 'around' turns it into an adjective, about that nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Jamaican is the adjective for things concerning or belonging to Jamaica, the island nation in the Caribbean Sea.

clue.text: Observe increasing feature of Arctic after time taken into account

indicators.note: something taken into the account is counted within it, so the time letter goes inside the phrase

parts.note: with warming, open water with no ice is ever more common there
T as an abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A climate report: look at the growing feature of the far north once time is factored in.
explanation.walkthrough: The feature is a grim joke on Arctic melting: open sea where the frozen cap used to be is what keeps increasing.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to see or perceive it, a straightforward synonym for observe as a verb.

clue.text: Article taken by boat? I should think so

parts.note: the indefinite article
a dhow is an Arab sailing vessel

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an item went by sea and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.definitionFit: And how! is an emphatic exclamation of agreement, meaning very much so, just like I should think so.

clue.text: Claim tailless river creature returned at a quick pace

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter of the verb is cut off

parts.note: to allege is to claim

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the creature is read right to left

parts.note: the otter lives along rivers

explanation.surface: A tall tale about an animal without a tail hurrying back up a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegretto is a musical tempo marking meaning fairly brisk, a little slower than allegro, so it describes a quick pace.

clue.text: A source of pain in past years

indicators.note: in tells us the letters lie inside the following two words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Sounds like a reminiscence about an old ache from long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, which is sore and so causes pain.

clue.text: French name, impressive thing to note

parts.note: slang: something great or fun is a gas
taken as written
N as an abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on a striking French name worth writing down.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaston is a common masculine first name in France, so it is an example of a French forename.

clue.text: Angelic figures? Grate I observed in church with them

indicators.note: things observed in a place are seen inside it, so the verb and pronoun sit within the other pieces

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
'em is the informal shortening of them
to grate is to rub harshly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A churchgoer is irritated by the carved angels around them.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three letters are church and the last pair 'em (them); the grating word and I sit inside 'em.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherubim is the plural of cherub, a winged angelic being often shown as a chubby child, hence angelic figures.

clue.text: Blessing reformed brute accepting one reduced sphere of action

indicators.note: a reformed brute has been remade, so its letters are recast with the added numeral

parts.note: taken as written
Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the last letter of the path word goes

parts.note: one's orbit is one's range of influence or activity

explanation.surface: A savage turns over a new leaf and settles for a smaller world.
explanation.walkthrough: Urbi et orbi, Latin for to the city and to the world, is the Pope's blessing given at Easter and Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the papal benediction addressed to Rome and the whole world, so it is a specific blessing.

clue.text: Your holiday was where?

parts.note: surface reading: a friend asking where you went on your trip
setter's reading: the reply-shaped question names a short break, plus the incredulous exclamation 'you went where?'

explanation.surface: A friend quizzes you on your holiday destination.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a short holiday and an exclamation of disbelief, so it suits a startled 'it was where?'
explanation.definitionFit: A getaway is a brief holiday or escape, and 'Get away!' is the British exclamation of amazed disbelief.

clue.text: Support song engrossing millions watching from home

definitions.note: adjective, as in an armchair fan

indicators.note: something engrossing another absorbs it entirely, so the support wraps the abbreviation

parts.note: an arch is a supporting structure
M for million
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A sports fan sings along with millions of others while watching the match on TV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' and 'watching' invite a stadium reading; the support is a piece of building.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair fan or critic follows the action from the comfort of home rather than taking part or attending.

clue.text: Auntie deadheaded quiet sweet-smelling plant

indicators.note: deadheading a flower removes its head, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: Auntie and the Beeb are both nicknames for the BBC
calm means quiet and still

explanation.surface: An aunt does some gardening, snipping off spent flowers among quiet fragrant plants.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie is the affectionate British name for the BBC, the national broadcaster, also called the Beeb.
explanation.definitionFit: Bee balm, also called bergamot or monarda, is an aromatic garden herb whose leaves smell sweet and citrusy.

clue.text: Sweet medication in water perhaps is served up

indicators.note: in a down entry, served up means the whole is read from the bottom upwards
in places the medicine inside the body of water

parts.note: a pool is an example of water
a pill is a dose of medicine

explanation.surface: A sugary medicine is dissolved in water and handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a hard sweet on a stick, so it is a type of sweet, the British word for a candy.

clue.text: Quick — agent's about to nod off

indicators.note: about means around, so the agent's letters surround the snooze

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
to nap is to doze or nod off

explanation.surface: An urgent warning that the secret agent is about to fall asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'has' rather than a possessive: the spy has a nap about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy means brisk and fast, as in make it snappy, so it fits quick as an adjective.

clue.text: Cites South-East, reflecting about kiss? This guy might

definitions.text: Cites South-East, reflecting about kiss? This guy might

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirror-wise, so the string is read backwards
about means surrounding, so the verb wraps the kiss

parts.note: to cite someone is to name them
X is the kiss at the end of a letter
compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A brash fellow name-drops the South-East and talks of a snog.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex Man is a British stereotype from the 1990s: a brash, newly prosperous working-class Tory voter from Essex in South-East England. The whole clue describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: The stereotype hails from the south-eastern county and is pictured as a boastful, flirtatious type, so citing it fits.

clue.text: Mistake that misdirects students

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a blunder or error
second, punning meaning: students at university are said to be up, and to slip them is to send them astray

explanation.walkthrough: Students are 'up' at university in old British usage; the cryptic second half reads the phrase as wrong-footing those students.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip-up is a careless error or minor blunder, a direct synonym for mistake as a noun.

clue.text: Foodstuff beginning to stick in regressive part of intestine

indicators.note: regressive means moving backwards, so the gut section is read from its end
in places the letter inside the bowel section

parts.note: the ileum is the final section of the small intestine

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the opening letter of stick

explanation.surface: A medical image of something lodged in a backward-moving gut.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a breakfast cereal of oats, nuts and dried fruit, so it is a kind of food.

clue.text: Artillery item capable of absorbing crushing force?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a short cannon that lobs shells at high angles
second meaning: the bowl in which a pestle grinds spices

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second definition as playful: the kitchen bowl takes the pounding of the pestle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a high-angle gun and the sturdy bowl used with a pestle for grinding.

clue.text: Cradles without front structural supports

indicators.note: without its front means the first letter of the beds is dropped

parts.note: cribs are cots or cradles

explanation.surface: Baby beds with no front panel, viewed as building frameworks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribs are curved members that brace a ship's hull, a vault or the chest, so they are structural supports.

clue.text: British writer commented endlessly about King

parts.note: to comment is to say something
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A British author keeps going on and on about the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, the Edwardian British short-story writer known for his wit.

clue.text: Exaggerated role by Phi in developing foremost of crosswords

indicators.note: developing means changing form, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; Phi is the setter's pseudonym

indicators.note: foremost of points to just the leading letter of the puzzle word

parts.note: the opening letter of crosswords

explanation.surface: The setter Phi talks up his own part in creating crosswords.
explanation.walkthrough: Phi is the setter of this puzzle, so the clue is a self-deprecating joke about overstating his role.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperbolic language overstates things for effect; hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration, so the adjective matches.

clue.text: Asian leader mostly fit to receive investment from European country and yen

indicators.note: receiving an investment means taking it in, so the shortened word holds the other letters

parts.note: to suit is to fit or be right for
the United Kingdom
Y is the symbol for the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: An Asian ruler, not quite fit, attracts British and Japanese money.
explanation.definitionFit: Aung San Suu Kyi led Myanmar's democracy movement and later its government, so she is an Asian political leader.

clue.text: Record boy being upset about attention, right?

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged lad surrounds the hearing word
upset means knocked over and jumbled, so the lad's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
to lend an ear is to pay attention
OK? means all right?

explanation.surface: Checking whether a lad is upset about being noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearbook is an annual publication recording the events of a year, so it is a kind of record.
